cards: How are animal viruses categorized?
By nucleic acid, capsid, and the presence or absence of an envelope
What are the three capsid shapes?
Helical, icosahedral, and complex, the complex one being the phage
Where does an animal virus get its envelope?
From the host cell membrane as the virus buds out of the cell
How does a phage get its DNA into a bacterium in the lytic cycle?
Viral lysozyme and a tail pin breach the wall and inject the DNA
How are new phages released at the end of the lytic cycle?
Viral lysozyme causes the host cell wall to burst open
What becomes of the phage DNA in the lysogenic cycle?
It integrates into the bacterial chromosome and becomes a prophage
What makes a prophage leave the bacterial chromosome?
A shock of some kind induces it to release and start a lytic cycle
What new trait can a lysogenic bacterium acquire?
The ability to make a toxin
Which kind of transduction goes with the lytic cycle?
Generalized transduction: random pieces of host DNA passed to other bacteria
Which kind of transduction goes with the lysogenic cycle?
Specialized transduction: all cells carry the same DNA from the host
Which phages use the chronic cycle?
Filamentous phages: flexible rods carrying single-stranded DNA
How do chronic-cycle phages penetrate without lysozyme?
Through compatibility between virion capsid proteins and host receptor proteins
What happens to the bacterium in the chronic cycle?
Virions are extruded without lysis and the bacterium's growth slows
How does an animal virus enter its host cell, unlike a phage?
The entire virion is engulfed rather than only the DNA being injected
What step must an animal virus undergo that a phage does not?
Uncoating, to release its genetic material inside the cell
How are animal virus virions released, unlike a lytic phage?
By budding, which may give the virus its envelope
Where are most DNA viruses replicated and budded from?
The nucleus of the host cell
Which DNA viruses multiply in the cytoplasm instead of the nucleus?
The poxviruses, which multiply in cytoplasmic factory areas
What is an acute viral infection?
A rapid course following the lytic cycle, as in colds and flu
What defines a persistent chronic viral infection?
Virus detectable in tissue, multiplying slowly, with mild or absent symptoms
Which two viruses are the examples of persistent chronic infection?
Human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis B virus
What defines a persistent latent viral infection?
A dormant, generally undetectable virus that can reactivate as recurrent infection
Which virus family is the example of persistent latent infection?
The herpesviruses
What form does latent herpesvirus DNA take?
An episome: in the nucleus but not integrated into the chromosome
What does oncogenic mean for a virus?
A persistent virus that causes cancer
What does teratogenic mean for a virus?
A virus that crosses the placenta and causes permanent developmental defects
Which two viruses are the teratogenic examples?
Rubella and cytomegalovirus
Which B cell malignancy of the jaw does Epstein-Barr virus cause?
Burkitt's lymphoma
Which cancer do papillomaviruses cause?
Cervical and penile cancer
Which cancer does hepatitis B virus cause?
Hepatic carcinoma, also called hepatocellular carcinoma
Which three families are the enveloped double-stranded DNA viruses?
Poxviruses, herpesviruses and hepadnaviruses
Which three families are the nonenveloped double-stranded DNA viruses?
Adenoviruses, polyomaviruses and papillomaviruses
Which family is the nonenveloped single-stranded DNA virus group?
The parvoviruses
What skin lesion gives the poxviruses their name?
Eruptive skin pustules, called pocks or pox, that leave scars
How is smallpox transmitted?
Inhaled airborne saliva, contact with pustule or scab material, and fomites
When is a smallpox patient most contagious?
During the early rash, when mouth spots break open and release virus
When is a smallpox patient no longer contagious?
Once all the scabs have fallen off
What is smallpox's place in the history of vaccination?
It was the first disease eliminated by vaccine
How is smallpox prevented?
Vaccination with vaccinia virus, a live virus vaccine
What do molluscum contagiosum lesions look like?
Small, smooth, waxy lesions on the genital area and thighs
How does mpox enter the body?
Through broken skin, the respiratory tract or mucous membranes
Which lymph finding is part of the early mpox illness?
Swollen lymph nodes, along with fever, aches, chills and exhaustion
What tool helps people find an mpox vaccine?
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention vaccine locator tool
Where are cowpox lesions usually found in humans?
Usually confined to the hands
What are the primary reservoirs of cowpox?
Rodents, with humans often infected by handling cats that met rodents
What cowpox vaccine exists?
A vaccine only for animals, used in Europe for circus and zoo animals
How do humans catch orf virus?
By handling infected sheep and goats: feeding, shearing or bites
What do all herpesviruses share in their behavior?
All show latency and cause recurrent infection
What does herpes simplex virus type 1 cause, per the herpesvirus list?
Fever blisters
What does herpes simplex virus type 2 cause, per the herpesvirus list?
Genital infections
Which herpesvirus infects salivary glands and viscera?
Cytomegalovirus
Which herpesvirus infects lymphoid tissue and causes infectious mononucleosis?
Epstein-Barr virus
Which two herpesviruses cause roseola?
Human herpesvirus 6 and human herpesvirus 7
Which herpesvirus causes Kaposi's sarcoma?
Human herpesvirus 8
Can herpes simplex spread when no lesions are visible?
Yes: genital herpes can be transmitted in the absence of lesions
Where does herpes simplex virus type 1 stay latent?
In the trigeminal ganglion
Where does herpes simplex virus type 2 stay latent?
In the lumbosacral spinal nerve trunk ganglia
What is herpetic whitlow?
Herpes simplex entering a skin break, usually infecting one finger
How is herpes of the newborn prevented at delivery?
Cesarean section if the mother has an outbreak at the time of birth
How is varicella zoster virus transmitted?
Respiratory droplets and contact with fluid from active skin lesions
When is varicella zoster virus most infectious?
In the day or two before any lesions develop, before the rash is seen
Where does varicella zoster virus hide after chickenpox?
It enters neurons and remains latent
What does reactivated varicella zoster virus cause?
Shingles, with vesicles localized to dermatomes along a nerve path
What does an unvaccinated child catch from a shingles patient?
Chickenpox, not shingles
What vaccine protects against varicella zoster virus?
A live attenuated vaccine for both chickenpox and shingles
What is the owl's eye effect?
An enlarged cytomegalovirus-infected cell whose nucleus holds a large inclusion
Which three groups get severe cytomegalovirus disease?
Fetuses, newborns and immunodeficient adults
Why is there still no cytomegalovirus vaccine?
Development is difficult because there is no animal model
How is Epstein-Barr virus transmitted?
Direct oral contact and contamination with saliva
What are the signs of infectious mononucleosis?
Sore throat, high fever, cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly
Where does Epstein-Barr virus lie dormant?
In B cells
What is the course of roseola?
Fever first, followed by a faint maculopapular rash
What does Kaposi's sarcoma look like?
Small, painless, discolored skin lumps that may spread to internal organs
Whose common tumor is Kaposi's sarcoma?
Patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome
What is unusual about the hepadnavirus genome?
It contains both double-stranded and single-stranded DNA
How much blood can transmit hepatitis B?
Minute amounts of blood or blood products
Why is hepatitis B a risk to health care workers?
Its very low infective dose: minute amounts of blood transmit it
What is the outcome for most people infected with hepatitis B?
Few overt symptoms, then they eventually develop immunity
What is the primary prevention for hepatitis B?
Vaccination with surface antigen made in cloned yeast
How are adenoviruses spread?
By respiratory and ocular secretions
Are adenoviruses oncogenic?
In animals, but not in humans
Who receives the adenovirus vaccine?
Some military personnel, vaccinated in training environments
How is human papillomavirus transmitted?
Through direct contact or contaminated fomites
How is cervical human papillomavirus disease detected early?
A Pap smear to screen for abnormal cervical cells
Which disease does JC virus cause?
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, destroying myelin-producing cells
Where does BK virus lie dormant?
In the kidney and the lining of the ureters and bladder
When does BK virus cause disease?
After renal transplants and immunosuppressive drugs
What disease does parvovirus B19 cause in children?
Erythema infectiosum, or fifth disease, with a rash on the cheeks
What can parvovirus B19 do to a fetus?
Cause severe fatal anemia, resulting in hydrops fetalis
Why is adeno-associated virus called defective?
It cannot replicate in the host cell without adenovirus
What is adeno-associated virus used for?
As a viral vector for human gene therapy
